narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped the scale above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. First, your family income bracket of lower-middle had the strongest influence, actually pushing slightly in favor of passing. However, this positive effect was outweighed by the next two factors. Your LSAT score of 24 was the second most important element and strongly pulled the prediction toward failure. Compared to the average score of 37 among accepted students, this lower performance signaled a higher risk of struggling with the bar. Third, your third-year school decile ranking of 2 (versus an average around 5.8 for accepted students) further increased the likelihood of failure by highlighting consistently lower relative academic standing.

Taken together, these elements led the model to conclude that the risk of not passing the bar was too high for admission. Gender and race played no role in this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation and consider ways to strengthen your academic record or gain additional legal experience before reapplying. This could meaningfully shift your profile in future applications. (218 words)
